title: Encoder vs. Decoder vs. Encoder-Decoder
oneLineScope: When and why to pick each of the three transformer families — encoder-only, decoder-only, and encoder-decoder — and how T5's text-to-text framing tried to unify them.
prose:
Where we are. You have now seen both siblings. The autoregressive-lm node showed the decoder-only transformer: causal mask on, encoder off, trained to predict each token from its left context alone — the GPT lineage, built for generation. The masked-lm node showed the encoder-only transformer: no causal mask, trained to fill in randomly blanked tokens from full bidirectional context — the BERT lineage, built for understanding. Both derive from the same full transformer described in the-full-transformer node, and both are simplifications of it. This node puts the three families on the same table — encoder-only, decoder-only, and encoder-decoder together — to answer the practical question: given a task, which architecture should you reach for, and why?

The gist, in one paragraph. The three transformer families differ in exactly one structural dimension: what mask, if any, goes on the self-attention score matrix, and whether a separate encoder feeds context into a causal decoder via cross-attention. Encoder-only removes the mask, training for understanding tasks where the full input is fixed. Decoder-only adds the causal mask and removes the encoder, training for generation tasks where text is produced left to right. Encoder-decoder keeps both: a full encoder reads the source with bidirectional attention, and a causal decoder generates the target while cross-attending to the encoder’s output — the natural design for sequence-to-sequence tasks like translation and summarization. The choice of architecture constrains the choice of training objective, which in turn constrains the tasks the model handles well.

Why it matters. From 2018 to 2023 the NLP landscape was a genuine three-way competition among these families. Knowing what each is structurally suited to — and what each cannot do — gives you the frame for understanding why encoder-only models dominated NLU benchmarks for two years, why encoder-decoder models remained the default for translation and abstractive summarization, and why decoder-only models eventually became dominant for general-purpose language modeling once scale arrived.

The three families, side by side

Encoder-only (the BERT family): a stack of \(L\) transformer blocks with no causal mask — every position attends to every other; the \(n \times n\) score matrix is fully populated. The output is a sequence of dense contextual representations, one per token, each informed by the entire sequence simultaneously. Pre-trained with the masked LM objective (and, in BERT’s original formulation, NSP — later found dispensable by RoBERTa). Naturally suited to understanding tasks: classification, named-entity recognition, extractive question answering — anywhere you need to map a fixed input to a label or a selected span. Cannot generate sequences autoregressively: with full bidirectional attention there is no principled way to decode token by token without reconstructing the masking at inference time.

Decoder-only (the GPT family): a stack of \(L\) transformer blocks with a causal (lower-triangular) mask — each position attends only to its predecessors and itself. Pre-trained with the next-token cross-entropy objective. Naturally suited to generation and in-context learning: open-ended text production, completion, and — at large scale — few-shot adaptation by prepending examples to the prompt. Cannot efficiently encode a complete bidirectional context for understanding tasks in the way an encoder-only model can, though it can be fine-tuned to do so.

Encoder-decoder (the original Vaswani et al. 2017 transformer, T5, BART): a full encoder reads the source sequence with bidirectional attention; a causal decoder generates the target, attending to the encoder’s output via cross-attention at each layer. Pre-trained with span-corruption objectives (T5) or denoising objectives (BART). Naturally suited to sequence-to-sequence tasks: machine translation, abstractive summarization, question generation — anywhere the output is a new sequence conditioned on a complete input sequence.

Family Attention pattern Pre-training objective Natural task fit Representative models

T5 and the text-to-text framing

Raffel et al. (2020) — T5, “Text-to-Text Transfer Transformer” — proposed an elegant unification: cast every NLP task as a sequence-to-sequence problem with a text input and a text output. Translation becomes “translate English to German: sentence”; sentiment becomes “sentiment: sentence” → “positive”; summarization is a straight seq2seq. By using one architecture (encoder-decoder), one objective (span corruption: replace contiguous spans with sentinel tokens and predict the missing spans in the decoder), and one loss function across all tasks, Raffel et al. could do large-scale controlled comparisons of architecture choices, pre-training objectives, and dataset compositions on the same footing. T5 was trained on C4 (Colossal Clean Crawled Corpus), a filtered version of Common Crawl totaling roughly 750 GB of text. The text-to-text framing is conceptually clean; whether it is efficient — using a full encoder-decoder to predict a single-word sentiment label — is a legitimate question, one T5 does not fully answer.

BART (Lewis et al., 2019) took a different approach to the encoder-decoder: pre-train by corrupting the input in various ways (token masking, deletion, permutation, text infilling) and training the decoder to reconstruct the original. BART proved especially effective on summarization and generative question answering, where the ability to reconstruct corrupted text transfers well to generating fluent output conditioned on a noisy or incomplete source.

The historical arc and what it implies

From roughly 2018 to 2020, encoder-only models dominated NLU benchmarks, and encoder-decoder models dominated seq2seq tasks. The decoder-only lineage was competitive on generation but seemed architecturally specialized. The arc shifted as scale arrived: decoder-only models at billion-parameter scale, trained on web-scale corpora, showed that in-context learning — adapting to new tasks by reading examples in the prompt, with no weight updates — was an emergent capability tied to model size rather than to architectural bidirectionality. GPT-3 (Brown et al., 2020) demonstrated this at scale, and the decoder-only paradigm became dominant for general-purpose language models. The encoder-decoder family retained a strong niche in structured generation tasks; the encoder-only family remains the standard for embedding-based retrieval and NLU where a single-pass representation is what is needed.

Those later developments — scaling laws, in-context learning — are the subject of subsequent nodes in this graph. Before reaching them, the next immediate topic is the one mechanism all three families share equally: the choice of tokenization. How a sequence of characters is carved into the discrete units that flow through any of these architectures — the tradeoffs of byte-pair encoding and WordPiece — is the subject of the tokenization-subword-units node directly ahead.

diagrams.caption: Three side-by-side mini-architectures showing the characteristic attention pattern of each transformer family: encoder-only (bidirectional), decoder-only (causal), and encoder-decoder (both).
diagrams.altText: Three columns side by side. Left column labeled 'Encoder-only (BERT)': a stack of blocks with a full grid of bidirectional self-attention arrows among all token positions. Middle column labeled 'Decoder-only (GPT)': a stack of blocks with a lower-triangular causal mask, only leftward arrows. Right column labeled 'Encoder-decoder (T5, Vaswani)': an encoder stack with bidirectional attention feeding via cross-attention into a decoder stack with causal attention. Each column labels its attention pattern and a representative model name.
diagrams.prompt: Structural side-by-side diagram of the three transformer families, three columns. Left column labeled 'Encoder-only (BERT)': a small stack of two or three block rectangles. Inside, draw a 4-by-4 grid of dots representing the attention matrix — all cells filled, no masking, labeled 'bidirectional: all attend to all'. Below the stack, a label '[CLS] → classification'. Middle column labeled 'Decoder-only (GPT)': same small stack of blocks. Inside, a 4-by-4 lower-triangular attention grid — only the lower triangle and diagonal filled, upper triangle empty/grey, labeled 'causal: left context only'. Below, a label 'next-token generation'. Right column labeled 'Encoder-decoder (T5, original Transformer)': two stacked sub-groups — an upper encoder section with a full bidirectional grid, and a lower decoder section with a lower-triangular grid plus a cross-attention connection (a double arrow) from the encoder output to the decoder. Below, a label 'seq2seq: translation, summarization'. Under each column, list one or two representative model names in muted grey. Keep it clean with generous spacing; structural diagram.
